items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S3895

 TITLE OF BILL :

An act to amend the social services law and the penal law, in relation
to enforcement of child day care safety and standards; to repeal
paragraph (b) of subdivision 12 of section 390 of the social services
law relating to the use of single family dwellings for family day care
or group family day care


 PURPOSE OF THE BILL :

This bill would enhance the availability of safe, affordable, and
accessible child day care; increase the child day care capacity in
group family day care homes; and improve quality enforcement for all
levels of child day care.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Section 1 of the bill would amend Social Services Law (SSL) §
390(1)(d) and (e) to amend the definitions of "group family day care
home" and "family day care home" to increase the maximum number of
children for whom care may be provided in group family day care homes
from ten to twelve and to provide that an assistant must be present
when nine or more children are being cared for. Section  would also
provide that there must be one caregiver for every two children under
age two in a family day care home, consistent with the requirements of
a group family day care home.

Sections 2 and 3 of the bill would amend SSL § 390(2)(a) and SSL §
390(2)(d)(ii)(A), respectively, to provide that the Office of Children
and Family Services (OCFS) may issue an initial child day care license
or registration that is valid for a period of up to two years and
subsequent licenses valid for a period of up to four years as long as
the provider remains substantially in compliance with applicable
statutes and regulations.

Section 4 of the bill would amend SSL § 390(3)(b) to delete a
provision permitting a child day care provider to avoid a sanction by
correcting certain regulatory violations within thirty days of
notification by OCFS. The bill enables OCFS, in appropriate instances,
to seek fines and/or revocation of the provider's license or
registration without having to wait thirty days.

Section 5 of the bill would amend SSL § 390(11)(c) to provide
additional exceptions to instances in which a child day care provider
may rectify a regulatory violation in order to avoid a sanction. The
bill authorizes OCFS to impose a sanction for the initial violation in
these serious situations even though the violation subsequently was
corrected. The bill would provide for a sanction where a provider or
staff has injured a child in care, failed to obtain necessary medical
attention for a child, used corporal punishment against a child,
failed to report suspected child abuse or maltreatment when required
to do so. or submitted a forged document to OCFS.

Section 6 of the bill would add a new paragraph (e) to SSL § 390(11)
prohibiting the issuance of a license or registration to a child day
care provider whose license or registration was revoked or terminated
during the previous two years, unless OCFS determines that licensure
or registration would not jeopardize in any way the health, safety, or
welfare of the children for whom care would be provided. The
prohibition also applies to a child day care provider facing
enforcement action who surrenders a license or registration in order
to avoid a suspension, revocation, or termination. The prohibition
will also apply to a child day care program that is fined on two
separate occasions for operating without a required license
or-registration.

Section 7 of the bill would repeal SSL § 390(12)(b), which limits the
ability of local governments to prohibit regulated family day care or
group family day care programs from operating in one, two or multiple
family dwellings.

Section 8 of the bill would amend SSL § 390-a(3)(b)(ix) to limit
mandated staff training on shaken baby syndrome to those day care
programs that legally may care for infants. The bill would exempt
registered school-age child care programs from the training
requirements, as those programs cannot care for infants legally.

Section 9 of the bill would add a new subdivision seven to SSL § 410-x
permitting a social services district to suspend an informal
legally-exempt provider from providing child care services funded
under the New York State Child Care Block Grant where the informal
legally exempt provider is under investigation by child protective
services as the subject of a report of child abuse or maltreatment.

Section 10 of the bill renumbers Penal Law (PL) § 260.30, as added by
Chapter 600 of the Laws of 1998, to § 260.31 for the purpose of
clarity, as two PL sections numbered 260.30 were enacted in 1998. In
addition, the renumbered section, pertaining to criminal
misrepresentation by a child day care provider, is amended to
specifically include an informal legally-exempt child care provider
within its scope. The types of prohibited misrepresentation are
expanded to include an intentional misrepresentation by a provider in
documentation required for enrollment to provide subsidized child care
or in documentation regarding compliance with minimum health and
safety standards. In addition, the bill adds a new provision to PL §
260.31 making it a class A misdemeanor for a person to provide child
day care if he or she is ineligible to receive a license or
registration under the new paragraph (e) of subdivision 11 of SSL §
390.

Section 11 of the bill would provide for an immediate effective date,
except for the PL amendments in section 10 of the bill, which would
take effect on November first.

 EXISTING LAW :

SSL §390 defines child day care and governs the licensing and
registration of child day care providers by OCFS. It includes
authority for suspension or revocation of a license or registration
and civil penalties against child day care providers who violate
applicable statutes or regulations. The holder of a license or
registration is entitled to a hearing before OCFS prior to the
imposition of any sanction. A child day care provider may avoid
imposition of a penalty for most regulatory and statutory violations
by correcting the violation. Even where the penalty imposed is the
loss of the provider's license or registration, the provider may apply
to OCFS for a new license or registration almost immediately.

SSL § 390-a sets forth standards and training requirements for child
day care providers. In 2004, legislation was enacted requiring
training on the shaken baby syndrome for all operators, program
directors, employees and assistants of child day care programs,
including school-age child care programs that cannot care for infants.

SSL § 410-x governs the use of child day care subsidies by social
services districts and requires providers of legally-exempt child care
who receive subsidy funds to meet minimum health and safety standards.
Informal legally-exempt child care providers are not required to be
licensed or registered by OCFS. Informal legally-exempt child care
providers must be enrolled with a social services district to be
eligible to provide subsidized child care.

Chapter 381 of the Laws of 1998 enacted PL § 260.30 pertaining to the
endangerment of vulnerable elderly adults:

Chapter 600 of the Laws of 1998 also enacted a PL § 260.30, known as
Jeremy and Julia's Law, which criminalized an intentional
misrepresentation by a child day care provider pertaining to the
number of children in care, the area of the home, facility or center
used for child day care, or the credentials of the provider and/or
staff where the misrepresentation substantially places the health or
safety of a child at risk. Such a misrepresentation, when made to a
parent, OCFS or law enforcement agency, is a class A misdemeanor.

Chapter 416 of the Laws of 2000 enacted the Quality Child Care and
Protection Fund as State Finance Law § 97-www. Penalties assessed
against child day care providers are deposited in the fund. Monies in
the fund may be used for grants to child day care providers for health
and safety purposes, for training of child day care providers' staff,
and for other activities to increase the availability and/or quality
of child day care programs.

 PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

Portions of the bill were previously introduced in 2004 as S.6642. A
substantially similar bill was introduced in 2008 as
S.4545-A/A.10662-A and was referred to the Assembly Social Services,
Children and Families Committee and the Senate Rules Committee.

 STATEMENT IN SUPPORT :

The availability of safe, affordable, accessible child care is
important to working families and to families that otherwise need
child care for a portion of the day or week. Quality child care
enormously benefits the development of children and should be
available to families seeking such care. This proposal would was
generated in response to these concerns and also results from
discussions arising from Governor Spitzer's Executive Order 12, which
directed OCFS to meet with representatives of child day care providers
and discuss improvements to the child day care system.

This proposal would expand the capacity of group family day care homes
by permitting the program to care for up to 12 children instead of the
current maximum of 10. A group family day care home could care for an
additional four school-age children during non-school periods instead
of the two additional children permitted under present law.  The
proposal would increase from seven to nine the number of children who
could be cared for by the operator of a group family day care home
without an assistant present. The proposal would also make consistent
the requirement that a group family day care home or a family day care
home must provide one caregiver for every two children under the age
of 18 months.

This proposal would enhance OCFS' ability to require child day care
providers to meet critical health and safety standards by further
limiting those instances where a provider who is in violation of a
statutory or regulatory requirement can avoid a penalty by merely
fixing the violation. In addition, a provider who has been penalized
by the revocation or termination of a license or registration would be
ineligible to receive a new child day care license or registration for
a period of two years unless OCFS determines that the health, safety,
or welfare of children in care would not be jeopardized in any way. A
provider who has been sanctioned for illegal operation within the
previous two years would also be ineligible for a license or
registration for two years. These provisions would deter child day
care providers from operating substandard or illegal programs by
increasing the potential consequences for statutory and regulatory
violations, while reducing the administrative burden for those day
care programs that are operating in compliance with statute and
regulations by extending the maximum term of renewal licenses and
registrations to four years instead of two years.

This proposal would repeal a provision that generally precludes local
governments from prohibiting the use of one or two family dwellings or
multiple dwellings for family or group family day care if OCFS
determines that the program meets the state's regulatory provisions,
which include health and fire safety requirements, for such programs.
SSL § 390(12)(a) includes a similar, more clearly worded restriction.
However, the repealed paragraph goes beyond paragraph (a) to enable
localities to preclude the operation of certain family or group family
day care programs that have been approved by OCFS.

This proposal also provides a local social services district with the
authority to suspend the enrollment of an informal legally-exempt
provider who is being investigated for child abuse or maltreatment.
As such, it provides much needed assistance to social services
districts that currently lack an effective means to safeguard a child
receiving subsidized child care from an informal legally-exempt
provider who is the subject of a report of abuse or maltreatment.

Finally, this proposal would strength Jeremy and Julia's Law
pertaining to misrepresentation by a child day care provider by
applying the provisions of Jeremy and Julia's Law to legally-exempt
providers and adding new provisions making it a crime for providers to
submit false information on the child care subsidy enrollment form. It
also makes it a crime for regulated and legally-exempt child care
providers to misrepresent compliance with minimum health and safety
standards. In addition, the proposal makes it a crime for persons who
have lost their license or registration to provide regulated child day
care to provide any form of child care, including legally-exempt care,
within two years after the loss of the license or registration.

 BUDGET IMPLICATIONS :

This proposal is not expected to have a significant financial impact,
although the funds deposited in the Quality Child Care and Protection
Fund may increase due to provisions expanding the circumstances where
OCFS may impose a penalty for statutory and regulatory violations
regardless of whether the violations have been rectified.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
This bill would take effect immediately, except for the PL amendments
in section 10 of the bill, which would take effect on November first.

previous two years would also be ineligible for a license or
registration for two years. These provisions would deter child day
care providers from operating substandard or illegal programs by
increasing the potential consequences for statutory and regulatory
violations, while reducing the administrative burden for those day
care programs that are operating in compliance with statute and
regulations by extending the maximum term of renewal of licenses and
registrations to four years instead of two years. This proposal would
repeal a provision that generally precludes local governments from
prohibiting the use of one or two family dwellings or multiple
dwellings for family or group family day care if OCFS determines that
the program meets the state's regulatory provisions, which include
health and fire safety requirements, for such programs. SSL
§390(12)(a) includes a similar, more clearly worded restriction.
However, the repealed paragraph goes beyond paragraph (a) to enable
localities to preclude the Operation of certain family or group family
day care programs that have been approved by OCFS. This proposal would
also amend §390(12)(a)-to include in that paragraph the prohibition on
restricting use that is currently provided for in paragraph (b). This
proposal also provides a local social services district with the
authority to suspend the enrollment of an informal legally-exempt
provider who is being investigated for child abuse or maltreatment. As
such, it provides much needed assistance to social services districts
that currently lack an effective means to safeguard a child receiving
subsidized child care from an informal legally-exempt provider who is
the subject of a report of abuse or maltreatment.

 BUDGET IMPLICATIONS :
This proposal is not expected to have a significant financial impact,
although the funds deposited in the Quality Child Care and Protection
Fund may increase due to provisions expanding the circumstances where
OCFS may impose a penalty for statutory and regulatory violations
regardless of whether the violations have been rectified.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
This bill would take effect immediately.
